column1: An otherwise healthy adult has confirmed GAS pharyngitis, no drug allergy and normal renal function. Give TWO MUMS first-line options with dose, frequency and duration.
column2:
Answer

  • Penicillin V 600 mg PO twice daily OR 300 mg PO three times daily for 10 days.
  • Amoxicillin 500 mg PO twice daily for 10 days.

Why

These are MUMS Canadian tablet regimens; the indication and duration matter as much as the drug name.

Watch for

Do not substitute the sinusitis amoxicillin frequency or assume every antibiotic lasts 5 days.

Source

MUMS 2024 printed pp. 8–10 (PDF pp. 21–23); Morgan and J.M. cases

column1: List THREE non-drug recommendations for an adult with painful GAS pharyngitis. Do not count acetaminophen or an herbal product.
column2:
Answer

  • Maintain hydration with cool or soothing fluids.
  • Use warm salt-water gargles if able to gargle safely.
  • Rest and reduce transmission with hand hygiene and avoiding shared drinking utensils.

Why

Comfort and transmission prevention accompany indicated antimicrobial treatment.

Watch for

Analgesics and medicated lozenges are pharmacologic, even if OTC.

column1: Morgan has confirmed GAS and a previous penicillin reaction with inability to breathe. Name a MUMS oral alternative, its adult dose and duration, and a check that could change your choice.
column2:
Answer

  • Clarithromycin 250 mg PO twice daily for 10 days is one MUMS alternative.
  • Check macrolide resistance, interactions and QT-risk factors before selecting it.
  • Avoid penicillin and do not choose cephalexin as if this were a benign delayed rash.

Why

A macrolide is not automatically suitable just because it is outside the penicillin class.

Watch for

The original case does not establish a universally best alternative independent of resistance and interactions.

column1: If azithromycin is selected for an adult with GAS, how does its MUMS schedule differ from clarithromycin?
column2:
Answer

  • Azithromycin 500 mg PO on day 1, then 250 mg once daily on days 2–5.
  • Clarithromycin is 250 mg PO twice daily for 10 days for this indication.

Why

The 5-day azithromycin regimen is an exception to the usual 10-day GAS course.

Watch for

Do not prescribe 500 mg twice daily for 10 days by blending the two drugs.

column1: Use MUMS pediatric GAS amoxicillin 40 mg/kg/DAY divided twice daily, maximum 1 g/day. A child weighs 20 kg; the supplied suspension is 250 mg/5 mL. Calculate mL per dose and the exact 10-day course volume.
column2:
Answer

  • 40 × 20 = 800 mg/day; 400 mg per dose.
  • 250 mg/5 mL = 50 mg/mL; give 8 mL PO twice daily.
  • 8 × 2 × 10 = 160 mL; no repeats for this acute course.

Why

The daily dose is below the stated maximum. The concentration is supplied for the exercise.

Watch for

CPS uses a different pediatric GAS amoxicillin regimen; this question explicitly tests MUMS 2024.

column1: A pregnant adult has confirmed GAS, normal renal function and no penicillin allergy. What reasonable first-line regimen can you retain? What should you monitor if breastfeeding?
column2:
Answer

  • Amoxicillin 500 mg PO twice daily for 10 days remains a reasonable MUMS regimen.
  • Pregnancy safety is supported by the linked NHS information; do not change to doxycycline simply because of pregnancy.
  • If breastfeeding, watch the infant for diarrhea, rash or thrush.

Why

The pregnancy statement is a separately labelled safety comparison, not an invented MUMS pregnancy table.

Watch for

Pregnancy does not automatically mean avoiding all antibiotics.

column2:

column1: For an adult with uncomplicated bacterial conjunctivitis and no ocular red flags, give ONE MUMS topical option with strength, frequency and usual duration.
column2:
Answer

  • One option is fusidic acid 1% ophthalmic drops: 1 drop in the affected eye(s) twice daily for 5–7 days.
  • MUMS lists several empirical options; fusidic acid is not the uniquely preferred choice for every patient.

Why

Specify ophthalmic formulation and affected eye(s).

Watch for

Do not apply a skin fusidic-acid preparation to the eye or automatically treat an unaffected eye.

column1: List THREE non-drug recommendations for uncomplicated infectious conjunctivitis.
column2:
Answer

  • Wash hands and avoid sharing towels or eye cosmetics.
  • Gently remove discharge using a clean single-use pad for each wipe.
  • Use a cool clean compress for comfort and stop contact lens wear while symptomatic.

Why

These address spread, discharge and discomfort.

Watch for

Artificial tears and antibiotic drops do not count as non-drug answers.

column1: A red eye is watery, follows a URI and has no pain, photophobia, visual loss or corneal abnormality. What changes if the working diagnosis is viral conjunctivitis?
column2:
Answer

  • Use supportive care and hygiene; routine antibiotics are not indicated.
  • Reassess if red flags or an atypical course develops.

Why

Discharge patterns guide probability but do not prove cause alone.

Do not prescribe an antiviral for ordinary adenoviral conjunctivitis.

column1: Jack has not improved after 2–3 days of correctly used topical therapy. What should you reassess before simply changing drops?
column2:
Answer

  • Recheck visual acuity, pain, photophobia, cornea and contact-lens history.
  • Review application/adherence and alternative diagnoses such as viral or allergic disease.
  • Arrange appropriate eye referral for concerning findings.

Why

Nonresponse may reflect a wrong diagnosis rather than antimicrobial resistance.

Watch for

Marked photophobia in Jack’s examination conflicts with his earlier denial and must be addressed.

column1: Why is a contact-lens wearer with a painful red eye and photophobia a different decision from uncomplicated conjunctivitis?
column2:
Answer

  • Consider microbial keratitis and arrange urgent eye assessment.
  • MUMS lists fluoroquinolone options for more serious/corneal or contact-lens-associated infection; treatment choice should accompany corneal assessment.
  • Avoid unsupervised ocular steroids.

Why

The risk is visual loss from corneal disease, not merely prolonged discharge.

Watch for

Do not use a routine conjunctivitis prescription to delay an urgent assessment.

column2:

  • Use 10 days in a child younger than 2 years.

The quantity is per DAY, not per dose.

column1: Stella weighs 8.5 kg. Select 80 mg/kg/DAY amoxicillin in TWO doses using 50 mg/mL liquid for 10 days. Calculate a complete medication line and exact course volume.
column2:
Answer

  • 8.5 × 80 = 680 mg/day; 340 mg/dose.
  • Amoxicillin 50 mg/mL oral suspension: 6.8 mL PO twice daily for 10 days.
  • Dispense at least 136 mL to cover 20 doses; choose an available package that supplies the course. No repeats.

Why

This reproduces the internally consistent seminar calculation. The stem fixes both the dose and the concentration.

Watch for

Do not divide 680 by 50 and use 13.6 mL at EACH administration.

Source

column1: How does MUMS AOM duration differ between a 13-month-old, a 5-year-old with uncomplicated AOM, and a 5-year-old with recurrent AOM or perforation?
column2:
Answer

  • 13 months: 10 days.
  • Age over 2 years, uncomplicated: 5 days.
  • Complicated, recurrent or perforated AOM: 10 days.

Why

A single drug does not imply a single duration for all patients.

A tympanostomy-tube otorrhea case is a separate topical-treatment decision.

column1: Stella’s penicillin history is clarified as a non-life-threatening delayed rash. Give one MUMS alternative regimen and distinguish this from anaphylaxis.
column2:
Answer

  • Cefprozil 30 mg/kg/DAY PO divided twice daily, maximum 1 g/day, is an option; at her age the AOM course is 10 days.
  • Cefuroxime is another MUMS option.
  • Immediate urticaria/anaphylaxis or a severe delayed reaction requires a different allergy assessment; do not generalize benign-rash eligibility.

Why

The reaction details determine which alternatives are reasonable.

Watch for

Do not equate diarrhea, a delayed mild rash, anaphylaxis and severe cutaneous reactions.

column1: Stella received amoxicillin two months ago. Does that automatically mean every beta-lactam is now ineffective? What must you check?
column2:
Answer

  • No. Assess prior response, relapse/reinfection, severity and timing, including whether exposure was within 30 days.
  • MUMS uses antibiotic exposure within 3 months as a high-dose risk factor; CPS specifically highlights recent amoxicillin within 30 days when considering amoxicillin/clavulanate.
  • Purulent conjunctivitis, treatment failure and allergy also change selection.

Why

This corrects the seminar’s blanket “change class within six months” rule.

Watch for

Do not make antibiotic class switching automatic from a date alone.

column1: List THREE non-drug measures to reduce recurrent otitis risk or support care.
column2:
Answer

  • Eliminate tobacco smoke exposure.
  • Avoid supine bottle feeding and bottles in bed.
  • Reduce prolonged pacifier use; discuss age-appropriate prevention and feeding practices.

Why

These are distinct from antibiotics, analgesics and vaccines.

Persistent effusion without acute infection is not an indication to keep switching antibiotics.

column1: Pain and fever have resolved, but middle-ear fluid remains at follow-up. What is the likely explanation and what needs monitoring?
column2:
Answer

  • Otitis media with effusion can persist after infection clears.
  • Do not extend antibiotics solely for asymptomatic residual fluid.
  • Monitor persistent hearing loss, speech/language concerns and duration; arrange hearing/ENT assessment when indicated.

Why

MUMS notes that post-AOM effusion commonly resolves over weeks to months.

Watch for

Redness or fluid alone is not proof of a new bacterial AOM.

column1: An adult has acute otitis externa, and you cannot verify that the tympanic membrane is intact. Name the MUMS product, dose and usual duration.
column2:
Answer

  • Ciprodex otic suspension, 4 drops into the affected ear twice daily for 7 days.
  • It contains ciprofloxacin 0.3% and dexamethasone 0.1%.

Why

MUMS recommends treating uncertain membrane integrity as a possible defect.

Watch for

Do not use an aminoglycoside-containing/ototoxic product or vinegar when a membrane defect is possible.

column1: List THREE non-drug instructions for otitis externa prevention and recovery.
column2:
Answer

  • Keep the canal dry during treatment.
  • Avoid cotton swabs and scratching/instrumentation.
  • After swimming, allow drainage and dry gently; discuss a suitable ear-protection plan.

Why

Acidifying drops require a confirmed intact membrane and are not automatically safe prevention.

Watch for

Do not insert objects deeply to clean the canal.

Diabetes and disproportionate persistent pain change the risk assessment.

Do not repeatedly extend ordinary drops without reconsidering invasive disease.

column1: Gerald has no clinical response by day 3, or develops orbital swelling and a visual change. What are the two different actions?
column2:
Answer

  • No response at about 3 days: reassess diagnosis, adherence, complications and treatment selection.
  • Orbital swelling/visual change, severe headache, toxicity or altered mental status: urgent referral/emergency assessment.

Why

Routine nonresponse and complication red flags have different urgency.

Watch for

Do not simply wait out the remaining antibiotic days when vision is threatened.

column2:

column2:

  • Use saline irrigation with safe water and clean equipment.
  • Avoid smoke/irritants and tailor bedroom/pet measures to actual triggers.

Specific trigger measures are more useful than an indiscriminate list of bans.

A sedating antihistamine and an herbal remedy are still pharmacologic.

A 2-year-old has acute ear pain and fever after a URI. Otoscopy shows a bulging tympanic membrane and middle-ear effusion. Which diagnosis best fits?

A. Otitis media with effusion alone
B. Otitis externa
C. Referred dental pain
D. Acute otitis media
column2:
Answer

D. Acute otitis media

Three differentials

  • Otitis media with effusion: fluid without acute inflammatory illness.
  • Otitis externa: canal inflammation and pain with tragal/pinna movement.
  • Referred dental pain: dental findings with an otherwise normal ear examination.

Red flags

  • Postauricular swelling/tenderness or a protruding pinna requires urgent assessment for mastoid complications.
  • Toxic appearance, neurologic changes or dehydration require prompt escalation.

Why

Bulging TM with acute inflammatory symptoms supports AOM. Effusion alone lacks acute inflammation; OE centers on the canal/tragal tenderness; referred dental pain does not explain the bulging TM. Red flags: Postauricular swelling/tenderness or a protruding pinna requires urgent assessment for mastoid complications. Toxic appearance, neurologic changes or dehydration require prompt escalation.

B. Tinea corporis
C. Nummular eczema

  • Rapid painful spread, fever or toxicity suggests a different/additional process requiring urgent assessment.

An active scaly advancing border favors tinea. A 62-year-old develops pressure in the chest and jaw while walking uphill that resolves with rest. Which explanation is most concerning and most consistent with this pattern?

A. Myocardial ischemia
B. Gastroesophageal reflux
C. Costochondritis
D. Panic disorder
column2:

Three differentials

  • Musculoskeletal chest pain: movement/palpation reproducibility may support it.
  • Panic-related symptoms: fear/autonomic context may support it only after serious causes are considered.

Exertional pressure with jaw radiation and relief with rest raises ischemic concern. Reflux is often meal/position related; costochondritis is often reproducible; panic requires its own supportive pattern. None is excluded solely by a brief stem. New or changing symptoms need timely assessment. Red flags: Current/prolonged or worsening rest pain, diaphoresis, syncope, dyspnea or instability requires emergency assessment. The combined pulmonary and systemic congestion pattern supports HF; confirm with appropriate investigations, including cardiac assessment/echo, rather than declaring the subtype from symptoms alone. A smoker has reproducible calf pain after walking a set distance, relieved by rest, reduced pedal pulses and ABI 0.78. Which diagnosis is most likely?

B. Lumbar spinal stenosis as the only explanation
C. DVT as the only explanation
D. Chronic venous insufficiency as the only explanation
column2:
Answer

A. Peripheral arterial disease

Three differentials

  • Neurogenic claudication: posture/flexion-related relief and spinal symptoms.
  • DVT: acute unilateral swelling/pain and thrombotic risk.
  • Venous insufficiency: dependent edema, varicosities and venous skin changes.

Red flags

  • Sudden pain with pallor, pulselessness, coldness, sensory loss or weakness suggests acute limb ischemia: emergency.
  • Rest pain, nonhealing ulcers or gangrene warrants urgent vascular assessment.

Why

Exertional claudication, reduced pulses and ABI below 0.90 support PAD. Neurogenic symptoms vary with posture; DVT more often causes acute unilateral swelling; venous disease often causes dependent edema/skin changes. Red flags: Sudden pain with pallor, pulselessness, coldness, sensory loss or weakness suggests acute limb ischemia: emergency. Rest pain, nonhealing ulcers or gangrene warrants urgent vascular assessment.

A patient has a high pretest probability of disease, but an initial test with limited sensitivity is negative. Which statement is best?

A. A second unrelated normal result guarantees exclusion
B. Reconcile the result with test performance, timing and clinical risk; further evaluation may be needed
C. The negative test always excludes disease
D. Pretest probability becomes irrelevant once any test is ordered
column2:
Answer

B. Reconcile the result with test performance, timing and clinical risk; further evaluation may be needed

Three differentials

  • The leading diagnosis: reassess whether the negative test could be false negative.
  • A close clinical mimic: look for discriminating history/exam findings.
  • A dangerous alternative: consider the consequence and urgency even if it is less likely.

Red flags

  • Instability or a time-sensitive presentation requires action despite an initially reassuring test.
  • A discordant result in a high-risk patient needs clinical reconciliation and a clear follow-up plan.

Why

A negative result changes probability according to test performance; it does not automatically reduce a high-risk presentation to zero. Consider timing, specimen quality, alternative testing and the consequence of missing disease. Red flags: Instability or a time-sensitive presentation requires action despite an initially reassuring test. A discordant result in a high-risk patient needs clinical reconciliation and a clear follow-up plan.

  • Nonbullous: S. aureus and/or S. agalactiae; bullous: toxin-producing S. agalactiae: GBS is substituted for GAS, and the bullous assignment is wrong.
  • Nonbullous: Staphylococcus aureus and/or Streptococcus pyogenes; bullous: toxin-producing S. aureus: Nonbullous impetigo can involve S. aureus/GAS; bullous disease is associated with toxin-producing S. aureus.

Why

Nonbullous impetigo can involve S. aureus/GAS; bullous disease is associated with toxin-producing S. aureus.

A patient’s persistent/double-worsening illness is assessed as uncomplicated acute bacterial sinusitis. Which usual bacterial set best fits?

A. Streptococcus pneumoniae; Haemophilus influenzae; Moraxella catarrhalis
B. Streptococcus pneumoniae; Pseudomonas aeruginosa; Staphylococcus aureus
C. Streptococcus pyogenes; Bordetella pertussis; Haemophilus influenzae
D. Pasteurella multocida; Staphylococcus aureus; Moraxella catarrhalis
column2:
Answer

A. Streptococcus pneumoniae; Haemophilus influenzae; Moraxella catarrhalis

Why each option fits or fails

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae; Haemophilus influenzae; Moraxella catarrhalis: Pneumococcus, H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis are the usual targets in this uncomplicated syndrome.
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae; Pseudomonas aeruginosa; Staphylococcus aureus: This substitutes organisms that do not represent the usual uncomplicated trio.
  • Streptococcus pyogenes; Bordetella pertussis; Haemophilus influenzae: GAS/pertussis do not form the usual uncomplicated sinusitis set.
  • Pasteurella multocida; Staphylococcus aureus; Moraxella catarrhalis: Pasteurella is a bite-exposure clue, not part of the usual uncomplicated sinusitis trio.

Why

Pneumococcus, H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis are the usual targets in this uncomplicated syndrome.
